text: For full effect of the Law on Food Safety

The Vietnam Union of Science and Technology Associations (VUSTA), in coordination with the Vietnam Association of Food Safety Science and Technology (Vinafosa), held a seminar on October 13 entitled "Contributions to the Draft Amendments to the Law on Food Safety," where participants called for improvements to regulations on food management, product declarations, traceability, and the allocation of responsibilities across the food supply chain.
The aim is to protect public health while creating a transparent and practical environment for production and business activities.
Previously, at its sixth session on September 24, the National Assembly Standing Committee discussed the draft amendments.
The National Assembly considered the draft for the first time at its second session in October, with adoption expected at its third session next May.
Professor Truong Xuan Lam, Vice Chairman of VUSTA, emphasized that food safety is essential to public health, quality of life, and sustainable development.

As food production and business models diversify, e-commerce expands, and processing, preservation, and distribution technologies evolve, revising the Law on Food Safety 2010 is necessary to improve regulatory effectiveness.
He called for stronger food safety inspections and post-market supervision, including better capabilities to detect, warn of, and address risks.
Controls should cover the entire process, from production and distribution to consumption, with inspection resources allocated according to the risk levels of different product categories.
The revised Law should also improve product management, declaration, and quality control, while strengthening traceability and digital transformation.
Professor Lam also stressed the need to clarify responsibilities and improve coordination among regulatory agencies.
Clearly defining the authority of each agency, management level, and supply chain participant would help eliminate overlapping responsibilities and improve enforcement.
State oversight should be complemented by businesses' own food safety controls, with greater attention to testing, risk assessment, early warnings, and public communication.
He also highlighted the role of experts and scientists in providing evidence and practical experience to help policymakers identify risks, assess policy impacts, and develop appropriate solutions.
Mr. Nguyen Van Nhien, Vice Chairman of Vinafosa, similarly called for improvements to food management, product declarations, and quality control.
Regulations should ensure safety while reflecting the characteristics and risk levels of different products, international practices, and Vietnam's actual conditions.
Unnecessary procedures should be removed without weakening businesses' food safety responsibilities.
He also emphasized the need to clarify the responsibilities of regulatory agencies and supply chain participants to reduce overlapping functions and improve coordination.
Alongside State oversight, businesses should strengthen their own controls, supported by testing, risk assessment, early warnings, and public education on food safety.

Mr. Huynh Minh Quang, Director of Safety, Health, Environment and Quality at the Asia Ingredients Group, proposed three guiding principles for the revised Law: risk-based management, responsibilities proportionate to the ability to control risks, and evidence-based regulation.
He said the Law should clearly distinguish between food safety, product quality, and declaration and labeling information.
Therefore, deviations from declared quality standards do not automatically constitute food safety risks.
Classification and enforcement should consider the nature and severity of violations, inherent risks, exposure levels, intended consumers, product functions, and compliance history.
Clear guidance is also needed for products with overlapping characteristics to ensure consistent enforcement.

Meanwhile, Ms. Tran Ngoc Anh, Director of External Affairs at Danone Vietnam, identified nine major concerns: expanding mandatory registration from four to five food categories could increase costs and overwhelm assessment agencies; lengthy licensing procedures could disrupt supply chains and constrain product innovation; transitional requirements and stability studies could burden businesses; imported food inspections could delay customs clearance and increase port congestion; approval requirements for foreign countries and production facilities could create trade barriers; businesses' right to self-assess conformity should be protected; mandatory micronutrient fortification should be scientifically justified; transitional labeling rules should allow continued use of compliant packaging and flexible information updates; and product definitions should reflect scientific characteristics to avoid misclassification and unnecessary procedures.
Danone Vietnam therefore recommended that the National Assembly, government, and drafting agency focus on three priorities.
First, adopt risk-based, science-driven management and eliminate unnecessary procedures.
Every registration, approval, testing or product modification requirement should demonstrate a corresponding public health benefit.

Danone recommended removing mandatory stability study reports from food registration dossiers and eliminating duplicated procedures, while strengthening risk-based post-market supervision, traceability, early warnings, and enforcement.
Second, ensure regulatory consistency, transparent procedures, and accountable enforcement.
Regulations should protect businesses' right to self-assess conformity where legally permitted, while maintaining corporate accountability and consistency with international commitments.

Registration procedures should be shortened, with clear maximum processing times, transparent assessment criteria, defined grounds for requesting supplementary documentation, and mechanisms for handling overdue applications.
Implementation should also be monitored to prevent conflicts of interest and improper conduct during administrative processing.
Third, assess policy impacts and prevent administrative procedures from disrupting supply chains.
Before expanding regulatory obligations, authorities should assess compliance costs, document processing and testing capacity, potential bottlenecks, reduced product shelf life, and supply shortages.
Transitional arrangements should reflect production and import cycles.
Businesses that submit complete dossiers on time should be allowed to continue operating while awaiting approval, except where food safety concerns warrant enforcement.
Participants agreed that relevant authorities should comprehensively consult with food manufacturers, importers, distributors, brand owners, and authorized organizations.
Guidance on product classification, declarations, data management, and post-market supervision should be developed and circulated for consultation early in the process.
They also called for reasonable transition periods covering existing dossiers, products already on the market, packaging and labeling, data, contracts, and authorization agreements.

VUSTA consolidated the seminar's recommendations into a report for submission to relevant authorities for consideration during the review and refinement of the draft Law before it was presented to the National Assembly.
VCCI IDENTIFIES FIVE MAJOR CONCERNS OVER FOOD SAFETY REFORMS

Despite being presented as a post-market management measure, the proposed product declaration process still requires regulatory authorities to receive and potentially review dossiers before products can circulate.
The Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI) argues that this could delay imports and create the impression that products have received government approval.
It recommends allowing businesses to sell products immediately after submitting declarations electronically, with automatic receipt and full corporate accountability.
The draft does not clearly use risk assessment results to determine which products require registration, declaration, or exemption.

The VCCI recommends making risk analysis the direct basis for determining the level of pre-market controls, adopting three risk categories rather than two, and maintaining existing risk-based inspection mechanisms until the new system is operational.
Broad product definitions and the addition of supplementary foods carrying health claims could bring hundreds of thousands of currently self-declared products into the registration system.
Proposed documentation requirements, including stability studies, could also increase costs to around VND500 million ($19,231) per product.
The VCCI recommends narrowing mandatory registration to genuinely high-risk products, limiting additional documentation, and removing blanket five-year renewal requirements.
Requiring compliance notices for every imported shipment could effectively eliminate the existing reduced inspection mechanism, which randomly checks no more than 5 per cent of eligible shipments.

Additional registration requirements for exporting countries and foreign production facilities could also increase pre-market controls from two to four layers, potentially delaying imports and creating trade barriers.
The VCCI recommends retaining risk-based inspection methods, introducing equivalence recognition, and allowing businesses to select designated testing organizations.
With nearly 400,000 products currently on the market, requiring businesses and regulators to complete new procedures within 24 months could overwhelm administrative and testing capacity.
The VCCI estimates that authorities would need to process nearly 800 dossiers per working day.

It recommends a unified 36-month transition period, preserving existing product declarations and registration certificates, and removing the proposed two-year limit on using existing packaging labels.
